title: Adobe Acrobat Automation Without Code in 2026
summary: Adobe Acrobat automation uses different tools: Action Wizard for manual triggers, PDF Services API for schedules, or connectors. Determine the right fit.
body_markdown:
## Creating your first Action Wizard action


Open Tools > Action Wizard, choose Create New Action, add your steps, save, then point it at a folder of PDFs. The trigger is you clicking Start, and that's the whole design: a person at a desktop decides when the batch runs.


Pick a name that says what the action does to a file, such as "OCR and flatten", because a vague name is how someone runs the wrong batch on a client folder three months from now.


### Adding steps and prompts in Action Wizard


Top to bottom, the editor lists steps in the order they run. Add each one from the left-hand categories, then set its options.


Where a step offers "Prompt User", that's your approval point: Acrobat stops and waits for a person before continuing, which is what you want for anything irreversible, such as redaction.


On a separate automation canvas the same anatomy shows at a glance: the step list runs down the left, and the selected step, "5. Page Audit", opens its configuration panel on the right.


That step sends text to OpenAI's GPT-6.1 Sol with a prompt asking for a 0-100 score and a 120-word summary.


Apply the same takeaway to Action Wizard: each step's settings are visible and editable on their own, so when output looks wrong you open that one step instead of rereading the whole flow.


If OCR comes after a step that searches text, the search runs against pixels and finds nothing, so put OCR first. Order matters.


### Running an Action Wizard action on a folder


Save the action, reopen it from Action Wizard, choose the files or folder, and run it. Then open a sample of the results before you trust the batch.


A messy file, such as a scan at an odd rotation or a password-protected PDF, is where a "set and forget" action quietly fails.


According to[Wonder-Ware](https://wonder-ware.com/2025/07/23/batch-processing-1000-pdfs-automation-tools-compared-adobe-action-wizard-vs-pdf-xchange/) , the payoff is time: Action Wizard processes **100 PDFs in about 3 minutes** . The same source puts a fast person doing it by hand at 50 minutes per 100 PDFs, and a slow one at 200 minutes.


That makes the manual route roughly 17 to 67 times slower.
